First, many research papers related to changes in customers' online shopping psychology have focused on customer anxiety. The security and privacy of online shopping environments are the most direct factors affecting customers' online shopping (Kim et al., 2008; Swaminathan et al., 1999).
Think of this as the "trust barrier": before a consumer can fully engage with a digital store, they must feel safe.

With more and more consumers choosing to shop online (Escobar-Rodríguez and Bonsón-Fernández, 2017), scholars generally believe that online customer experience (OCE) and online shopping experience (OSE) are important reasons affecting online shoppers' purchase behavior in the Internet environment (Trevinal and Stenger, 2014).

Second, regarding customers' external influencing factors, it has been found that the interface, navigation design style and commodity types of shopping websites may lead consumers to become “crazy” shoppers (Wu et al., 2016).
Here, the design of the digital environment acts as a psychological lever.
Among them, the design of a website platform with strong stimulation and effective visual sense has the effect of increasing consumers' return rate to the website (Hasan,
In other words, a visually engaging site doesn't just sell once; it creates a habit loop that brings customers back. Furthermore,
the different experiences of using a touch screen or mouse will also turn them into hedonistic customers rather than customers with a simple shopping demand (Chung et al., 2018).

This distinction is crucial: a "hedonistic" shopper is seeking pleasure and entertainment, whereas a "simple shopping demand" customer is purely utilitarian. The tactile interaction of a touchscreen can shift a user from the latter to the former, making the act of browsing itself enjoyable.

In addition, online reviews of customers who have completed purchases affect the purchase behavior of potential consumers (Wang et al., 2019a, b); customer reviews are regarded as an important factor in product sales (Lingreen et al., 2013; Sun, 2012).
This represents a form of social proof, where the experiences of past buyers serve as a guide for future ones.

More and more researches are examining the factors influencing online shopping from the behavior data of shoppers. However, the aforementioned literature has not considered the relationship with the commodity information of the website; the greater the online commodity page value (the average value for a web page that a user visited before completing an e-commerce transaction), the richer the service content. Therefore, this paper forecasts the influence of consumers' shopping behavior from real online shopping big data.

2.3 Summary
The literature review reveals that decision-making in SSCs, from the perspective of customer behavior intention, has great research value, especially in the context of big data changing the interaction between suppliers and customers (Feng and Shanthikumar, 2018). Suppliers can use data-driven tools to improve operational decision-making, service quality and meeting customer demand (Cohen, 2018). Although there are studies on the influencing factors of online shopping behavior, few have analyzed the SSC and consumer behavior from the perspective of big data, which is a research gap that this paper aims to fill. Based on the decision-making in SSCs, the Stackelberg game approach is used to analyze the relationship between providers, integrators and consumers in SSCs.

3. Methodology
3.1 Demand-side model
3.1.1 Feature selection theory. Feature selection can be divided into two categories according to the type of feature selection and the degree of correlation between the classifiers: filter method and encapsulation method. Because of the close relationship between the feature selection process and the classifiers, the encapsulated feature selection method can often achieve better results. The encapsulation feature selection method was first proposed by John et al. (1994). The encapsulation method directly takes the performance of the learning algorithm as the index for evaluating the feature subset, which is the biggest difference between the encapsulation method and the filter method. The encapsulation method is
JEIM

iterated repeatedly, and the time efficiency of the encapsulation method is lower than that of the filter method. However, the accuracy of the encapsulation method is obviously better than that of the filter method. There are many methods to evaluate features in encapsulation feature selection, including decision tree (DT), naive Bayesian classifier (NB), K-nearest neighbor method (KNN) and logistic regression (LR). This study selected the random forest (RF) model for feature selection.

3.1.2 Random forest. RF is an ML algorithm consisting of multiple classification regression trees. First, the bootstrap sampling technique is used to extract N training sets from the original samples; second, a cart decision tree is constructed for each training set, and a forest composed of N cart DTs is generated; thirdly, $m(m < M)$ are randomly selected from all M feature variables, and the features of the best training set are selected according to the minimum Gini index to branch the internal nodes; finally, the output of the set NDT is “voted” on, and the class with the most votes is used as the decision result of the RF.

In RF algorithm, the Gini index is used to measure the effect of feature segmentation. Assuming there are K classes in sample D, its Gini index is:
$$
\mathrm{Gini} (D) = 1 - \sum_ {k = 1} ^

\left(\frac {| C _ {k} |}{| D |}\right) ^ {2}
$$
In the formula, $C_{k}$ is the sample subset of class k in D, and K is the number of classes. If sample set D is divided into M parts after a segmentation, sample set D is divided into M parts: $D_{1}, D_{2}, \ldots, D_{m}$ . So, the Gini index of this segmentation is:
$$
\mathrm{Gini} _ {\text {split}} (D) = \frac {| D _ {1} |}{| D |} \mathrm{Gini} (D) _ {1} + \dots + \frac {| D _ {m} |}{| D |} \mathrm{Gini} (D _ {m})
$$
The Gini index is inversely proportional to the segmentation effect. The importance of all features can be ranked by calculating the average decreasing Gini index. The larger the value is, the more important the feature is.

3.2 Supply-side model
3.2.1 Stackelberg game. Game theory, as a mathematical theory to study how multiagent systems make decisions for themselves or their groups, is widely used in economics, operational research, computer science and other disciplines (Wang et al., 2019a, b). Among them, the Stackelberg game model, with master–slave structure, was put forward by the German economist Stackelberg in 1934. A Stackelberg game is a two-phase complete information sequential-move game, which has the characteristics of sequence. Strategically, the two parties make their own decisions in the light of the others' to ensure the maximization of their own interests under the other party's strategies, so as to reach Nash equilibrium (Kang et al., 2012).

In the Stackelberg game model, the party that makes the decision first is called the leader. After the leader, the remaining players (followers) make a decision according to the leader's decision. Then the leader adjusts his/her decision according to the followers' decisions, until the Nash equilibrium is achieved. This paper uses this game model to analyze the relationship between service providers (SP) and service integrators (SI).

3.3 Features of big data samples
Currently, most companies collect and store large amounts of data on their customers and keep records of all their past transactions. Many companies will make most operational decisions based on data. This paper uses a big data set (Sakar et al., 2018) of UCI Open (http://open.uci.edu/) online shopping intention (purchase or not), which is composed of behavioral data
Data-driven online service supply chain

information of 12,330 different customers in a year (see Table 1), including both customers' numerical features (e.g. “administrative,” “administrative duration,” “information” and “related products”) and category features (e.g. “operating systems,” “browser,” “traffic type,” “weekend”), which contain not only the real access information of user behavior intention but also the relevant situations of special holidays in a year.

To understand the scale and nature of this dataset, let's break down what these features actually represent. We are looking at a rich tapestry of user interactions, divided into two main types: **numerical** and **categorical**.

**Numerical features** are quantitative metrics that tell us *how much* or *how long* a customer engaged with specific parts of the website. For instance, "Administrative" counts the number of pages a customer visits related to product account management. This is a direct indicator of intent: if a user is spending time managing their account or viewing specific product details, they are likely in the consideration or decision-making phase of the purchase journey. Similarly, "Administrative duration" measures the total time spent on these pages in seconds. Time is a powerful proxy for engagement; a customer who spends 3,000 seconds on product pages is significantly more invested than one who bounces after 10 seconds. Other numerical metrics like "Bounce rate" and "Exit rate" provide insights into user satisfaction and friction points, while "Page value" offers a direct economic signal of the potential revenue associated with those visits.

**Categorical features**, on the other hand, classify the context of the visit. These are qualitative labels that help us understand *who* the customer is and *how* they arrived. For example, "Operating systems" and "Browser" tell us about the technical environment of the user, which can influence how the website loads and performs. "Traffic type" reveals the marketing channel that brought the customer in (e.g., via a banner ad, SMS, or direct entry), which is crucial for evaluating the effectiveness of different marketing strategies. "Visitor type" distinguishes between new and returning customers, a key distinction in customer lifetime value analysis. Finally, features like "Weekend" and "Month" capture temporal patterns, allowing us to see if shopping behavior spikes during specific times of the year or on weekends.

From the earlier description, it can be seen that the dimension of consumer online shopping behavior data is too large, which will lead to a large feature space, for which the data are easy to over fit. At the same time, more features will bring more redundant features and irrelevant features. Therefore, more dimensions of the data do lead to the data providing more information, and a proper feature dimension is essential (Song et al., 2019a, b). These problems will inevitably lead to the performance of classification algorithms declining. Generally, the performance of the classifier increases with the number of features, but decreases after increasing to a certain extent; this phenomenon is called the Hughes phenomenon (Hughes, 2003). Therefore, this study attempts to find the most critical factor to improve the service quality of SSC from the big data related to customer behavior intention and then find the optimal pricing scheme.

Let’s pause here to unpack a critical concept in machine learning: **The Hughes Phenomenon**.

You might intuitively think that "more data is always better." In many cases, this is true. However, when dealing with high-dimensional data (many features), we run into a counter-intuitive problem. Imagine you are trying to identify a specific person in a crowd. If you only look at their height, you might guess correctly some of the time. If you add their weight, your accuracy might improve. But if you start adding 50 other irrelevant details—like the exact shade of their shoelaces, the number of freckles on their left arm, or the specific brand of their watch—your model becomes overwhelmed. It starts to "memorize" the noise (the irrelevant details) rather than learning the true pattern (the person's identity). This is **overfitting**.

The **Hughes Phenomenon** describes exactly this trade-off. As you add more features to a classification algorithm, the model's performance initially improves because it has more information to work with. However, once the number of features exceeds a certain threshold relative to the number of samples (customers), the "curse of dimensionality" kicks in. The feature space becomes so vast and sparse that the algorithm struggles to find meaningful boundaries between classes. It begins to fit the random noise in the data rather than the underlying signal, causing performance to drop.

This is why **feature selection** is not just a nice-to-have, but a necessity. We must identify the "most critical factors"—the features that truly drive customer behavior and revenue—while discarding the redundant or irrelevant ones. By doing so, we reduce the complexity of the model, prevent overfitting, and ultimately improve the accuracy of our predictions. In this study, the goal is to sift through this large dataset to find the optimal subset of features that best predicts customer behavior, which will then inform the optimal pricing scheme for the Service Supply Chain (SSC).

Relevant SSC research reveals that service outsourcing is common (Liu et al., 2018). Many enterprises with resource advantages will become leaders. They can become a bridge between service providers and customers, outsourcing the orders of customers to suppliers, processing and pricing the services of service providers and finally providing them to customers. Thus, a common SSC structure is formed: "upstream service provider (SP)—service

To fully understand the dynamics of this system, we must look beyond just the raw data and consider the strategic value of the platform itself. Specifically, the **page value**—a metric representing the visibility, traffic, and brand prestige of the online platform—should be considered a critical variable in the Online Service Supply Chain (OSSC). Think of page value as the "prime real estate" of the digital world; just as a shop with a high-traffic location can charge more for the same goods, a platform with high page value influences how services are priced and consumed.

In light of this, the study builds a theoretical model of the Service Supply Chain (SSC) from the supply side. By taking page value as the **visualization level**—essentially, the lens through which we view the market's attractiveness—the model aims to quantify exactly how this visibility impacts the **optimal pricing** strategies within the OSSC. In other words, we are trying to answer a specific question: How does the "shine" of the platform change the price tags on the services sold through it?

To ground this theoretical model in reality, we look at relevant SSC research, which reveals that **service outsourcing** is a very common practice (Liu et al., 2018). Why is this so prevalent? It comes down to resource advantages. Many enterprises do not have the internal capacity to handle every aspect of service delivery. Instead, those with specific resource strengths often step into the role of **leaders** or orchestrators.

These leaders act as a strategic **bridge** between two distinct groups: the service providers (who create the service) and the customers (who need it). The leader’s job is to manage the flow between them. They take orders from customers, outsource the actual execution of those orders to specialized suppliers, process and set the prices for the services provided by those suppliers, and finally deliver the finished service to the end customer.

Let's pause here to unpack what these equations are telling us. We are looking at the "sweet spot" for the system—specifically, the values for price ($p^*$) and information quality ($e^*$) that maximize profit. Notice the common denominator in these formulas: $(b k \eta - \theta^2)$. This term is critical. It represents the balance between the market's responsiveness to price ($b$), the efficiency of the service ($k, \eta$), and the customer's sensitivity to information quality ($\theta$). If the sensitivity $\theta$ becomes too high relative to the other factors, the denominator shrinks, which mathematically implies that the optimal price and quality levels must adjust significantly to maintain stability and profitability.

It is easy to prove that for the leader of the SSC, that is, the integrator, the information service quality makes the integrator set a higher price and obtain a higher optimal profit. It also increases with the sensitivity coefficient $\theta$ , leading to proposition 2.

The improvement of information service quality will lead to the improvement of the best pricing of service products by integrators, but ultimately the improvement of the best profit. The higher the sensitivity of customers to the quality of information service, the greater the improvement of pricing and optimal profit that SI can obtain.

Here, the logic flows from cause to effect. The "integrator" (SI) acts as the leader in this supply chain. The proposition asserts a positive feedback loop: as the SI invests in better information service quality, they can justify a higher price point ($p^*$). Why? Because customers who are highly sensitive to information quality ($\theta$) perceive greater value in that quality. Therefore, the SI can capture more of that perceived value as profit. Essentially, if your customers care deeply about the quality of the information you provide, you have the power to charge more and earn more, provided you actually deliver that quality.

5.2 Limitations and future research
Although this paper yielded some interesting results, there are some limitations, highlighting several directions to explore in the future. First, this study constructs an algorithm model for feature selection of big data, but the sample dimensions are still limited so the ranking of influencing factors obtained by the four classifiers is consistent; more kinds of online shopping data can be considered for analysis in future studies. Second, this study is based on a specific research background (only one supply chain upstream service provider and one service provider). In reality, SIs often have multiple agents at the same time. Future studies should consider the supply chain pricing strategy of multiple SPs and one (or more) SI.
